# Agent-Editing World Model: Rethinking World Modeling for LLM Agents

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/09/2609.28416.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Proposed Agent-Editing World Model (AEWM) focusing on modeling reasoning and action effects on task progress rather than tool response simulation
- Introduced Action Judge to classify decisions as Critical, Exploratory, or Noisy
- Developed State Revision to edit noisy reasoning-action continuations based on observed history
- Created EditAct integrating AEWM capabilities with real execution to directly modify state for improved decision-making
- Trained AEWM across multiple domains with mid-training and supervised fine-tuning
- Demonstrated AEWM and AEWM-RFT outperform strong baselines across benchmarks and agent backbones

### Method
AEWM models how reasoning and actions influence future task progress by combining Action Judge for decision classification and State Revision for editing noisy continuations, integrated via EditAct which modifies underlying state during execution; trained with mid-training and supervised fine-tuning across diverse domains, plus rejection sampling fine-tuning (AEWM-RFT) on verified trajectories.

### Result
AEWM achieved 70.5% macro-F1 on Action Judge benchmark, surpassing baselines by 10.6 points; EditAct improved average scores by 3.2–6.7 points across six benchmarks and three agent backbones; AEWM-RFT further improved performance by 2.2–2.6 points over Self-RFT without online guidance.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to LLM-based autonomous agents, agent memory architectures, LLM planning and reasoning, tool use, agent self-improvement, evaluation benchmarks, and prompt engineering; advances agentic frameworks and autonomous AI system paradigms.

# Can AI agents conduct open-ended AI research? Early evidence from two case studies

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/07/2607.27191.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduced shadow evaluations where AI agents attempt open-ended research questions from unpublished papers graded by original authors
- Conducted two case studies with frontier AI agents on NeurIPS 2026 submissions over six days
- Identified five key failure modes in AI agents performing open-ended research tasks
- Demonstrated agents can autonomously complete engineering tasks but fail at critical research lifecycle components
- Provided reproducibility by releasing expert reviews, survey responses, agent repositories, and logs

### Method
Shadow evaluations involving AI agents tackling central open-ended research questions from unpublished high-quality papers, with grading by original authors over extended compute time.

### Result
Agents successfully completed engineering without human help but failed to make substantial progress on research questions, leading to unambiguous rejection by authors; failure modes included poor judgment, uncreative problem-solving, ineffective backtracking, poor resource awareness, and instruction drift.

### Relevance
High interest for LLM-based autonomous agents, agentic frameworks, agent evaluation and benchmarks, agent self-improvement and reflection, and prompt engineering for agent control; provides early evidence on capabilities and limitations of current AI agents in open-ended research contexts.

# Learning Meta-Skills for Agent Harness Design in Test-Time AI4AI

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/09/2609.38143.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduced Meta-Skill concept to specify when and what support an agent needs
- Developed a Builder model that learns to construct execution environments for a Target agent without changing model weights
- Created a skill bank from Target's execution feedback to enable reusable environment construction
- Demonstrated improved agent performance on Harness-Bench and NewtonBench using learned meta-skills
- Showed that meta-skills outperform direct resource delivery to the Target agent
- Highlighted potential for system-level self-improvement by learning to build better environments

### Method
The Builder learns meta-skills from the Target agent's execution feedback on a development set, forming a frozen skill bank that guides environment construction for unseen tasks without modifying either model's weights.

### Result
Using the full meta-skill bank, agent performance improved by 8.95 percentage points over no-skill construction and by 12.02 points over direct resource delivery, demonstrating the effectiveness of executable support in enhancing agent execution.

### Relevance
High interest due to focus on LLM-based autonomous agents, agentic frameworks, agent self-improvement, and agent evaluation; aligns with interests in multi-agent systems, planning, reasoning, and agent control; introduces a novel paradigm for improving agent environments at test-time.

# AssemblyWorld: Rethinking 3D Assembly with General-Purpose Agents

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/09/2609.40353.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduced AssemblyWorld, an interactive 3D environment for evaluating general-purpose agents on 3D assembly tasks
- Created AssemblyWorldBench with 100 assembly tasks across 80 diverse objects including furniture and industrial parts
- Demonstrated agents perceive part geometry via 2D rendered views without direct mesh access
- Evaluated eight agent systems revealing significant performance gaps between open-source and closed-source agents
- Analyzed agent behavior showing how assemblies are revised and residual positioning errors remain
- Provided a benchmark to assess interactive assembly agents and the gap between approximate and precise 3D reconstruction

### Method
Developed a 3D interactive environment where agents manipulate rigid parts guided by visual inputs such as images or manuals, perceiving parts through 2D views and evaluated assemblies geometrically; benchmarked multiple agent systems on diverse assembly tasks.

### Result
The strongest agent achieved 80.9% part accuracy and 59.4% complete assembly success; open-source agents performed substantially worse than closed-source peers; analyses revealed common failure modes and residual errors in assembly precision.

# BlenderRAG: High-Fidelity 3D Object Generation via Retrieval-Augmented Code Synthesis

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/05/2605.00632.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduced BlenderRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation system for Blender code synthesis

- Demonstrated improved compilation success rates from 40.8% to 70.0% using retrieval during generation
- Achieved higher semantic alignment (CLIP similarity from 0.41 to 0.77) without fine-tuning or specialized hardware

### Method
BlenderRAG retrieves semantically similar multimodal examples (text, code, image) from a curated dataset during code generation with state-of-the-art LLMs to improve output quality and consistency.

### Result
Significant improvements in executable Blender code generation quality, with higher compilation success and semantic alignment, enabling practical deployment without additional training or hardware requirements.

### Relevance
The approach enhances LLM reasoning and tool use by integrating retrieval-augmented generation, relevant for AI agents and multi-agent systems requiring reliable code synthesis and multimodal memory integration.

# 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/10/2610.22341.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduces 3DCodeVerse-2M, a curated dataset of executable 3D code with source files, assets, descriptions, and verification records.
- Develops a multi-agent DAG harness that generates and refines 3D programs using execution checks, spatial measurements, and visual feedback.
- Provides empirical baselines and component-level analyses, with practical guidance for 3D coding agents.

### Method
Collect and convert open-source 3D code, generate programs with coding agents, and use a multi-agent generation-and-refinement harness with automated verification; fine-tune open models for evaluation.

### Result
Fine-tuning on the dataset improves open-source models’ 3D coding capabilities. The harness achieves a 90% win rate over Claude Design (3D Object) in pairwise human evaluations when both are used by Claude Opus 5.5.

### Relevance
High relevance to autonomous and multi-agent systems: the work presents an agent framework that uses tools, automated evaluation, and iterative refinement. It also contributes a benchmark-like dataset and evaluation evidence for agent performance.

## Summary
### Contributions
- Reformulated VLA pretraining as goal-conditioned reinforcement learning using language instructions as goals
- Introduced PRTS, a system learning unified embeddings approximating log-discounted goal occupancy for goal reachability
- Developed a role-aware causal mask integrating goal-reachability supervision into VLM backbone with minimal overhead
- Pretrained on large-scale diverse manipulation and embodied-reasoning data (167B tokens)
- Achieved state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks including LIBERO variants and real-world complex tasks
- Demonstrated significant improvements in long-horizon, contact-rich, and zero-shot novel-instruction robotic tasks

### Method
PRTS employs contrastive reinforcement learning to learn embeddings where the inner product of state-action and goal embeddings estimates goal reachability probability, integrating this supervision into a vision-language model backbone via a role-aware causal mask, enabling intrinsic goal reachability awareness for improved reasoning and action prediction.

### Result
PRTS achieved state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks such as LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv, and a suite of 14 real-world complex tasks, with notable gains in execution success and long-horizon planning, especially in contact-rich and zero-shot novel instruction scenarios.

### Relevance
PRTS advances AI agents and multi-agent systems by embedding goal reachability into vision-language-action models, enhancing temporal task progress understanding and reasoning; its approach to goal-conditioned reinforcement learning and embedding design is relevant for tool use, LLM reasoning, and practical AI engineering in agentic systems.

## Archive

## Summary
### Contributions
- Developed DexRoam system for learning mobile bimanual dexterous manipulation from egocentric whole-body human demonstrations
- Created a tracker-free human motion capture system using consumer VR headset and head-mounted stereo camera without external trackers
- Designed three explicit alignment stages (embodiment, action-semantic, temporal) to map human motion to robot action space preserving fine-grained whole-body motion
- Enabled joint learning of human and robot demonstrations with standard vision-language-action (VLA) policies
- Demonstrated significant improvement in policy success rates using human demonstrations across different VLA backbones

### Method
DexRoam captures continuous whole-body human manipulation demonstrations via a tracker-free system using VR headset and stereo camera, then applies embodiment, action-semantic, and temporal alignment stages to map human motion into robot action space, allowing joint learning with VLA policies.

### Result
Human demonstrations improved average success rates from 29% to 56% on GR00T N1.7 and from 32% to 57% on pi0.5, matching robot-only training with half the robot demonstrations; ablations confirmed each alignment stage is essential.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to humanoid robotics, whole-body control, robot learning from demonstration, VLA models, dexterous manipulation, robot perception, and sim-to-real transfer; represents a significant advance in embodied AI and physical robot dexterity.

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/09/2609.11875.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Identifies and addresses the transition realizability gap in vision-language-action robotic manipulation.
- Proposes UniMPA, a unified model integrating memory, prediction, and action via an action-grounded transition interface.
- Introduces Persistent-Selective Future Prediction to resolve transition ambiguity by modeling intended future state evolution.
- Develops a Visual-Action Memory Bank to ground predicted transitions in historically executable evidence, reducing prediction-execution mismatch.

### Method
UniMPA model combining persistent latent streams and selective pixel streams for future state prediction, coupled with dual memory banks (Visual-Action and Action-Visual) to ensure physical executability and context-aware action refinement.

### Result
Improved robotic manipulation by effectively bridging the gap between visual prediction and physically realizable actions, enabling context-adaptive and historically grounded transition modeling.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to vision-language-action models, robot learning for manipulation, embodied AI, and physical world understanding; aligns with interests in humanoid robotics, robot perception, sim-to-real transfer, and foundation models applied to robotics.

# Latent Action as Intention Enables Efficient Future Imagination for World Action Models

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/08/2608.24882.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduces LAWA, a WAM architecture using compact latent actions as future intentions for efficient test-time imagination
- Develops a discrete tokenizer with action-free pre-training for manipulation-centric codebook targets
- Jointly denoises continuous latent states anchored to executable action chunks, omitting future-video branch at inference
- Achieves state-of-the-art success rates on RoboCasa with improved generalization and lower latency compared to Fast-WAM and Joint-WAM
- Demonstrates competitive zero-shot robustness on LIBERO-Plus and superior real-world task performance
- Shows that retaining future imagination via latent actions balances performance, generalization, and latency effectively

### Method
LAWA uses a discrete tokenizer enhanced by action-free pre-training to produce manipulation-centric codebook targets, then jointly denoises continuous latent states anchored to these targets with executable action chunks, enabling efficient future imagination without generating future observations at inference time.

### Result
LAWA achieves 65.6% and 80.8% average success rates on RoboCasa in few-shot and full data settings, outperforming Fast-WAM by 9.6 and 4.5 points respectively, while reducing inference latency by 42.9%. It maintains performance comparable to Joint-WAM and shows strong zero-shot robustness on LIBERO-Plus and superior real-world task results.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to humanoid robotics, whole-body control, embodied AI, robot learning from demonstration and reinforcement learning for manipulation, vision-language-action models, robot perception, sim-to-real transfer, foundation models in robotics, and dexterous manipulation. The work advances efficient and generalizable robot control models with practical latency improvements.

# LIBERO-PeRM: Benchmarking Personalized Robotic Manipulation

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/10/2610.22372.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduces LIBERO-PeRM, a controlled benchmark separating manipulation task completion from preference satisfaction.
- Defines a taxonomy of language-expressible preferences covering motion, skill, and user-profile choices.
- Provides five task suites with 312 tasks, paired demonstrations, metadata, and automatic preference-satisfaction metrics.
- Evaluates zero-shot preference following, learning from demonstrations, generalization, composition, and conflict handling.

### Method
Builds on LIBERO with a procedural pipeline that generates paired demonstrations with and without preferences; evaluates vision-language-action policies under varied training and prompting strategies.

### Result
Current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while supervised fine-tuning enables preference learning. Mixed training improves retention of non-preference behavior and contextual-prompt performance, but can weaken motion-preference learning. Generalization, preference composition, and conflict handling remain challenging.

### Relevance
Strong fit for embodied AI, robot learning from demonstration, manipulation, and VLA models. The benchmark offers a systematic way to study how robots adapt behavior to user preferences, though it focuses on simulated tasks rather than humanoid control or real-world transfer.

# DLAM: Distributional Latent Actions with Temporal Constraints

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/07/2607.27138.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduces DLAM, a distributional latent-action model representing transitions as diagonal Gaussians.
- Proposes normalized composition and reversal constraints over equal-gap triplets to improve temporal consistency.
- Incorporates variance composition with shared-correlation coefficients to model dependence between adjacent transitions.
- Freezes encoder and trains flow-matching policy for joint generation of latent transitions and robot actions.
- Demonstrates improved temporal consistency and reconstruction on held-out videos compared to baselines.
- Shows enhanced policy performance on MetaWorld MT50, LIBERO, and real-world manipulation tasks under controlled transfer.

### Method
DLAM models latent action transitions as diagonal Gaussian distributions with reconstruction conditioned on reference frames. It applies normalized composition and reversal constraints to both mean and variance over equal-gap triplets, using a shared-correlation coefficient for variance composition. The encoder is frozen and a flow-matching policy is trained to jointly generate mean transition sequences and robot actions.

### Result
DLAM achieves more temporally consistent latent dynamics, stronger direct and cumulative reconstruction on held-out videos, and improved policy performance on multiple robotic manipulation benchmarks compared to existing latent-action baselines.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to vision-language-action models, robot learning for manipulation, sim-to-real transfer, embodied AI, and physical AI, aligning with high-interest areas such as humanoid robotics, robot perception, and reinforcement learning for manipulation.
note.title: DLAM: Distributional Latent Actions with Temporal Constraints

# LeFlow: Generative Latent Flow Planning for World Models

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/08/2608.24855.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduces LeFlow, a reusable latent trajectory prior for planning in latent world models
- Recasts planning as conditional latent trajectory generation in latent dynamics space
- Uses a rectified-flow model to generate future latent paths between current and goal states
- Employs an inverse dynamics decoder to convert latent transitions into action sequences
- Demonstrates order-of-magnitude reduction in planning time with improved success rates on pixel-control benchmarks
- Provides code for reproducibility and further research

### Method
LeFlow learns a latent trajectory prior operating in the latent dynamics space of a frozen world model, using a rectified-flow model for conditional latent trajectory generation and an inverse dynamics decoder to produce action chunks, verified by autoregressive rollout in the world model.

### Result
LeFlow achieves consistent success-rate improvements and reduces planning time by an order of magnitude compared to iterative action-space optimization across four major goal-conditioned pixel-control benchmarks.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to embodied AI, robot learning for manipulation and locomotion, vision-language-action models, robot navigation and environment mapping, robot perception, sim-to-real transfer, and foundation models applied to robotics, aligning with the target profile's high interest areas.
note.title: LeFlow: Generative Latent Flow Planning for World Models

# Rethinking Representations for World-Action Modeling

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/09/2609.38163.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Identified limitations of reconstruction fidelity and pre-trained perceptual features alone for effective policy learning in world-action models
- Proposed ReWAM, a representation-centric world-action model using pre-trained DINO features
- Introduced Feature Calibration and Temporal Representation Bottleneck to create compact world states for dynamics modeling
- Developed Action-Grounded Representation Shaping to allow policy-driven representation encoding while world model learns dynamics

### Method
ReWAM builds on pre-trained DINO features and organizes them via Feature Calibration and a Temporal Representation Bottleneck; it uses Action-Grounded Representation Shaping to route action-loss gradients to the bottleneck, enabling policy influence on representation encoding without generative video pre-training.

### Result
ReWAM achieved 93.6% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and an average score of 12.29 with 8.28% success rate on RoboDojo using ~600 hours of embodied pre-training data.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to embodied AI, robot learning for manipulation and locomotion, robot perception, sim-to-real transfer, and foundation models applied to robotics, aligning with high interest areas in humanoid robotics, embodied reasoning, and physical world understanding.

World-action models (WAMs) jointly learn robot policies and predict how the world evolves. Many recent WAMs (Bi et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Ye et al., 2026c; Yuan et al., 2026b) build on pre-trained video generators and predict future observations in the latent space of a video variational autoencoder (Video-VAE). These models inherit dynamics priors from large-scale generative video pre-training, but their latent spaces are typically optimized for visual reconstruction. Such spaces may preserve fine-grained appearance detail

# Structured 4D Latent Predictive Model for Robot Planning

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/07/2607.01166.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduces a Structured 4D Latent Predictive Model encoding holistic 3D scene representations.
- Enables prediction of scene evolution in 3D consistent latent space conditioned on observations and textual instructions.
- Demonstrates improved multi-view coherence and 3D consistency over state-of-the-art video-based planners.
- Integrates a goal-conditioned inverse dynamics module translating predicted futures into executable robot actions.
- Achieves superior performance on complex manipulation tasks and robust generalization to novel visual conditions.
- Validates effectiveness on real-world robotic platforms with enhanced planning and execution capabilities.

### Method
Develops a structured latent predictive model that encodes and predicts 3D scene dynamics in a 4D latent space, conditioned on observations and instructions, combined with a goal-conditioned inverse dynamics module for action execution.

### Result

# T2-z: Test-Time Optimization of Environment Latents for Robotic World Models

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/10/2610.22364.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduces T2-Z, a learnable environment latent that captures hidden environmental variation without labels.
- Alternates between learning general action-conditioned dynamics and optimizing environment latents through world prediction.
- Adapts to unseen environments by optimizing a newly initialized latent from test-time interactions while keeping the world model frozen.
- Shows latent inference can work from a single test-time interaction trajectory.

### Method
Train a robotic world model across environments using alternating optimization: update dynamics with latents fixed, then update latents with the model frozen. At test time, optimize a fresh environment latent from one or more interaction trajectories.

### Result
Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks, object prediction error fell from 15.20 to 7.00 and action success rose from 33.73% to 72.96%. The learned latents represent individual and combined environmental factors.

### Relevance
High relevance to embodied AI, robot learning, and sim-to-real adaptation: the method helps robots reason about hidden physical properties and environmental rules when predicting action outcomes.

# Zero-WAM: In-Context World-Action Modeling from Human Videos for Open-Ended Task Generalization

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/08/2608.26103.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduced Zero-WAM, a causal video-action model for zero-shot cross-task generalization in robotic manipulation.
- Developed an automatic pipeline to convert robot trajectories into semantically matched human videos, creating the HumanGen dataset with 74.2K human-robot pairs across 8.6K tasks.
- Proposed an in-context future chunk prediction (IFP) training objective to enhance task information extraction from video prompts and suppress shortcuts.
- Demonstrated significant performance improvement over baselines with 47.0% success on seven unseen RoboTwin 2.0 tasks.
- Validated real-world generalization to complex multi-object, long-horizon, and fine-grained manipulation tasks guided by human videos.

### Method
Zero-WAM leverages in-context learning by using human videos as task specifications to guide robotic manipulation, trained on the HumanGen dataset with an in-context future chunk prediction objective to enforce task understanding from video prompts.

### Result
Achieved a 47.0% average success rate on seven unseen RoboTwin 2.0 simulation tasks, outperforming the strongest video-action baseline by 29.5 percentage points; demonstrated effective real-world generalization to complex manipulation scenarios.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to humanoid robotics, embodied AI, robot learning from demonstration, vision-language-action models, sim-to-real transfer, and dexterous manipulation, addressing key challenges in zero-shot task generalization and physical world understanding.

## Summary
### Contributions
- Identification of a fundamental trade-off between generalizable transit and precise manipulation in existing World Action Models (WAMs).
- Proposal of HarmoWAM, an end-to-end WAM that unifies predictive and reactive control for both generalizable transit and precise manipulation.
- Introduction of a Process-Adaptive Gating Mechanism to coordinate between predictive and reactive action experts.
- Demonstration of strong zero-shot generalization across unseen real-world robotic tasks with variations in background, position, and object semantics.
- Significant performance improvements over prior state-of-the-art VLA models and WAMs by margins of 33% and 29%, respectively.

### Method
HarmoWAM leverages a world model providing spatio-temporal physical priors to condition two complementary action experts: a predictive expert using latent dynamics for iterative action generation, and a reactive expert inferring actions from predicted visual evolution. An adaptive gating mechanism dynamically switches between these experts to balance generalization and precision.

### Result
HarmoWAM achieves strong zero-shot generalization in six real-world robotic tasks across three unseen environments, significantly outperforming prior state-of-the-art models by 33% and 29%.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to embodied AI, robot learning for manipulation, vision-language-action models, physical AI, and dexterous manipulation, aligning with high-interest areas such as humanoid robotics, robot perception, and sim-to-real transfer.

# FlowWAM: Optical Flow as a Unified Action Representation for World Action Models

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/07/2607.13017.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduces FlowWAM, a dual-stream diffusion framework using optical flow as a unified video-native action representation.
- Proposes leveraging optical flow to align action representation with pretrained video generators for improved control and prediction.
- Demonstrates FlowWAM's ability to operate in two modes: policy mode for action prediction and world-model mode for future video generation.
- Enables pretraining on large-scale action-unlabeled video datasets by extracting flow from raw videos without action labels.
- Achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboTwin manipulation tasks with success rates over 92%.
- Improves trajectory accuracy by 18.4% on WorldArena world modeling benchmark.

### Method
FlowWAM employs optical flow as a unified action representation within a shared pretrained video generator using a dual-stream diffusion framework, enabling both action prediction and world modeling by generating or guiding flow sequences.

### Result
FlowWAM significantly outperforms existing baselines in manipulation and world modeling tasks, achieving high success rates on RoboTwin and the best EWMScore on WorldArena with notable improvements in trajectory accuracy.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to humanoid robotics, robot learning for manipulation, embodied AI, vision-language-action models, robot perception, sim-to-real transfer, and foundation models applied to robotics, aligning well with the target profile's high interest areas.

# Perceive, Predict, and Plan: a Unified World Action Model for Egocentric Dexterous Manipulation

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/10/2610.22363.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Unifies 3D hand and camera reconstruction, action-conditioned visual prediction, and goal-directed manipulation planning.
- Uses a structured 3D action representation to connect visual observations with dexterous actions.
- Demonstrates unified training benefits across perception, prediction, and planning.

### Method
P$^{3}$-WAM adapts a pretrained video diffusion transformer using shared base weights, modality-specific components, bidirectional visual-action attention, and randomized modality visibility. It supports Perceive, Predict, and Plan modes, with planning conditioned on an image, language instruction, and optional visual goal.

### Result
Outperforms specialized baselines in 3D hand reconstruction and action-conditioned video prediction across four datasets. It also produces more instruction-adherent, goal-directed manipulation videos than video-generation baselines, with improved planning quality under vision-language model evaluation.

### Relevance
High: directly addresses embodied AI, robot learning for dexterous manipulation, visual-action modeling, and foundation models for robotics. The work focuses on egocentric hand manipulation rather than humanoid whole-body control, and evaluates generated videos rather than physical-robot execution.

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduces Interleaved Vision-Language Reasoning (IVLR) framework with explicit multimodal traces
- Develops a native multimodal transformer to generate and utilize interleaved textual and visual task traces
- Creates pseudo-supervision by segmenting demonstrations and captioning stages with vision-language models
- Demonstrates high success rates on long-horizon robotic manipulation benchmarks (LIBERO, SimplerEnv-WidowX)
- Shows necessity of combining text and vision modalities for effective planning and execution
- Analyzes robustness of the trace representation under execution perturbations and partial trace corruption

### Method
IVLR uses an explicit intermediate representation called a trace that alternates textual subgoals with visual keyframes over the task horizon. A multimodal transformer self-generates this trace from initial observations and instructions, then conditions a closed-loop action decoder on the trace, instruction, and current observation. Pseudo-supervision is constructed by temporally segmenting demonstrations and captioning each segment with a vision-language model.

### Result
Achieved 95.5% average success on LIBERO benchmark, including 92.4% on the long-horizon LIBERO-Long subset, and 59.4% success on SimplerEnv-WidowX. Ablations show full interleaved traces outperform text-only or vision-only traces significantly. Execution perturbation tests indicate moderate robustness to local trace corruption and execution drift.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to AI agents and practical AI engineering by providing an interpretable multimodal planning representation that integrates language reasoning and visual grounding. The approach supports long-horizon task planning and execution in robotic manipulation, aligning with interests in multi-agent systems, tool use, LLM reasoning, and evaluation methods.

### Contributions
- Introduces ChunkAct, an action chunking method for agentic robotics.

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/07/2607.05377.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduced Cortex, a bidirectionally aligned embodied agent framework for long-horizon manipulation tasks.
- Standardized manipulation subtasks into 32 canonical skill primitives with tractability principles.
- Automatically annotated over 4k hours of open-source video and generated 30 hours of simulation data for training.
- Developed an event-balanced sampling strategy and harness engineering to handle planning ambiguity during subtask transitions.
- Demonstrated superior performance over monolithic baselines on Libero-long and RoboTwin benchmarks.
- Enabled zero-shot completion of unseen real-world long-horizon tasks by combining generalist VLM with fine-tuned VLA.

### Method
Cortex uses a customized planning interface to convey executable subtask plans from a high-level vision-language model (VLM) to a low-level vision-language-action model (VLA), leveraging standardized skill primitives and tractability principles in data generation, event-balanced sampling, and task-context-based harness engineering during inference.

### Result
Cortex outperforms monolithic baselines by 3.1% on Libero-long and 4.1% on RoboTwin benchmarks and enables zero-shot completion of complex unseen real-world long-horizon tasks, such as multi-stage chemistry experiments.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to embodied AI, vision-language-action models, robot learning for manipulation, and dexterous manipulation, aligning with high-interest areas in humanoid robotics, physical AI, and foundation models applied to robotics.

# CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/10/2610.22362.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduces CoDA, a framework that co-evolves simulation data generation and robot action policies through shared memory.
- Uses validated policy-failure diagnoses to create programs for reproducing challenging environments and training policies.
- Introduces Text2potential, which turns diagnoses into staged potentials for dense action-chunk value supervision while preserving the optimal policy under standard shaping assumptions.
- Uses measured learning progress to guide environment generation and program refinement.

### Method
Iterative simulation-based manipulation training: a vision-language critic diagnoses failures, shared heterogeneous memory compiles diagnoses into environment and training programs, and learning progress guides refinement.

### Result
Across four manipulation task families, out-of-distribution success rose from 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning to 27.6%, 9.5 percentage points above the strongest closed-loop baseline at the same generation budget. On LIBERO-Pro, 15 rounds increased success from 25% to 84% under position perturbations and from 1% to 76% under instruction perturbations.

### Relevance
High relevance to embodied AI and robot learning for manipulation. The work combines simulation, vision-language diagnosis, and policy learning to improve robustness to environmental and instruction shifts.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to AI coding assistants, agentic coding workflows, AI-assisted code review and refactoring, prompt engineering for code generation, AI pair programming, IDE integrations, and autonomous software engineering agents, representing a significant advancement in AI-assisted formal software verification.

# Structurally-bounded Agentic Graph Exploration for Evidence-Grounded Scholarly DeepSearch

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/08/2608.24809.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduces Crase, a bounded and inspectable agentic framework for scholarly search
- Implements a 1.5-hop citation neighborhood expansion with pruning based on entailment support
- Employs a recency-aware random walk for ranking candidate papers
- Provides explicit and fixed candidate set and stopping conditions before inference
- Demonstrates up to 3x recall@50 improvement over proprietary deep research agents at one-third the cost
- Validates approach on LitSearch and a 500K-paper arXiv benchmark

### Method
Crase queries a search engine once for seed papers, expands them along their 1.5-hop citation neighborhood, prunes citation edges lacking entailment support, and ranks remaining papers using a recency-aware random walk, making the candidate set and stopping condition explicit and fixed before inference.

### Result
Crase outperforms proprietary deep research agents by up to 3x recall@50 on LitSearch and an arXiv benchmark corpus, while operating at roughly one-third of the computational cost.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to LLM-based autonomous agents and agentic frameworks, particularly in agentic retrieval-augmented generation and agent evaluation; introduces a novel, structured agentic approach to scholarly search aligning with interests in agent memory, planning, and tool use.

# The Forward-Backward Disconnect: State Dynamics, Credit Assignment, and Biological Grounding in Neural Computation

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/08/2608.19995.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Identification of the forward-backward disconnect in neural computation between diverse forward dynamics and less diversified credit assignment methods
- Development of a taxonomy categorizing neural model families by state-dynamics structure, credit-assignment mechanism, and biological grounding
- Analysis of the asymmetry between forward computation diversity and training method concentration on gradient-based approaches
- Insight that closing the disconnect requires better alignment among state dynamics, credit assignment, and computational substrate
- Comprehensive survey across multiple neural architecture families including static, recurrent, attention-based, state-space, continuous-time, implicit, spiking, biologically plausible, and neuromorphic models

### Method
The authors perform a conceptual and theoretical analysis to develop a taxonomy and characterize the disconnect by reviewing and categorizing existing neural architectures and training methods along three coupled axes: state dynamics, credit assignment, and biological grounding.

### Result
They demonstrate that while forward neural dynamics have diversified significantly, scalable learning methods remain concentrated on gradient-based credit assignment, highlighting a fundamental asymmetry that limits progress and suggesting that future advances require integrated alignment of dynamics, learning mechanisms, and biological plausibility.

### Relevance
HIGH INTEREST: The paper addresses fundamental AI theory and learning mechanisms, proposes a new conceptual framework for understanding neural computation architectures, and is relevant to novel neural network architectures, interpretability, mechanistic understanding, and theoretical AI alignment.

- Introduces fixed-query oscillator attention as a novel attention mechanism based on Kuramoto synchronization dynamics.
- Demonstrates that oscillator attention replaces softmax exponentiation and global reduction with physical equilibration dynamics.
- Provides theoretical guarantees of unique and globally attractive fixed points for the attention mechanism across physical realizations.
- Empirically shows oscillator attention outperforms softmax on keyword spotting and subject-verb agreement tasks at minimal oscillator dimension.
- Shows oscillator attention narrows performance gap with softmax on causal language modeling as oscillator dimension increases.
- Offers a mathematically grounded blueprint for implementing accurate attention on energy-constrained physical substrates.

### Method
Replaces traditional softmax attention with a fixed-query oscillator attention mechanism using Kuramoto-Lohe synchronization dynamics, where queries are fixed anchors on a sphere and oscillators evolve to encode attention weights via cosine similarity, requiring no exponentiation and minimal global operations.

### Result
Oscillator attention achieves better or comparable performance to softmax attention on various NLP tasks, with theoretical guarantees of convergence and suitability for energy-efficient physical hardware implementations.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to novel neural network architectures with broad applicability, fundamental AI theory, emergent capabilities in large models, and provides a new paradigm for attention mechanisms aligned with physical substrate constraints.

# DEFault++: Automated Fault Detection, Categorization, and Diagnosis for Transformer Architectures

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/04/2604.28118.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduced DEFault++, a hierarchical diagnostic technique for transformer faults
- Developed DEFault-bench, a benchmark with 3,739 labeled fault instances across 7 transformer models and 9 tasks
- Created DEForm, a transformer-specific mutation testing method to generate fault data
- Proposed Fault Propagation Graph (FPG) to organize runtime behavior measurements at component level
- Combined prototype matching with supervised contrastive learning for interpretable diagnosis
- Demonstrated improved developer repair accuracy in a user study with 21 practitioners

### Method
DEFault++ performs fault detection, categorization into 12 transformer-specific fault types, and root-cause identification among 45 mechanisms by measuring runtime behavior of individual transformer components organized via a Fault Propagation Graph. It uses prototype matching and supervised contrastive learning for interpretable diagnosis. Training and evaluation leverage DEFault-bench, created through DEForm mutation testing across multiple transformer models and tasks.

### Result
DEFault++ achieved AUROC > 0.96 for fault detection and Macro-F1 of 0.85 for categorization and root-cause diagnosis on encoder and decoder architectures. In a developer study, repair action accuracy improved from 57.1% without DEFault++ to 83.3% with its support.

### Relevance
The work provides a detailed, component-level fault diagnosis framework for transformer architectures, enabling precise fault localization and repair guidance. Its hierarchical, interpretable approach and benchmark creation are valuable for practical AI engineering, especially in developing reliable agentic systems and tools that depend on transformer-based LLM reasoning and memory components.

# Attention over noisy examples: generalization and memorization in the exponential Hopfield network

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/10/2610.22191.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Transfers noisy-example learning from archetypes to the exponential Hopfield network, whose zero-temperature update is softmax attention over training examples.
- Derives a closed-form overlap with an unseen archetype using an effective attention entropy, extending the majority-rule result of the pairwise model.
- Shows that a temperature window suppresses interference between archetypes, allowing the learnable number of archetypes to grow as exp(c√N).
- Identifies memorization as a random-energy-model freezing transition in which attention concentrates on the nearest training example; reports corresponding diagnostics on MNIST and fashion-MNIST.

### Method
Signal-to-noise analysis of exponential Hopfield retrieval from multiple noisy examples per archetype, combined with a random-energy-model analysis of softmax weights and empirical diagnostics on MNIST and fashion-MNIST.

### Result
The unseen-archetype overlap is erf(1/√(2ρ_eff)). In a widening inverse-temperature window, load interference becomes exponentially small and capacity can scale as exp(c√N). At higher concentration, retrieval fails through memorization near β√(N(1−r²)) ≃ √(2 ln M), rather than through a spin-glass phase; fashion-MNIST accuracy can improve beyond this threshold by reading out local sub-prototypes.

### Relevance
High interest: provides theoretical insight into attention as a learning and retrieval mechanism, generalization versus memorization, and capacity in a Hopfield architecture. It is a focused theoretical advance rather than a broad new intelligence paradigm.

- Challenges the traditional 'circuit' ontology for understanding neural networks, especially LLMs
- Introduces representational drift as a fundamental obstacle to fixed-weight circuit interpretations
- Proposes a co-selectionist view of circuits as emergent units defined by correlated gradients
- Synthesizes neuroscience insights (plasticity, neurotrophins) with neural network interpretability
- Outlines three interpretability eras: exploratory, mechanistic, and prosaic
- Suggests 'diffuse computation' and denoising operations as promising new explanatory frameworks

### Method
Conceptual synthesis combining neuroscience findings, mechanistic interpretability research, and dynamical systems theory to critique and extend the circuit-based understanding of neural networks.

### Result
Argues that fixed, modular circuits are insufficient to explain LLM function due to noise and representational drift; proposes viewing circuits as dynamic, co-selected structures that move together under training dynamics, and calls for new theories of diffuse computation and developmental motifs to better capture neural network internals.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to interpretability and mechanistic understanding of neural networks, fundamental AI theory, emergent capabilities in large models, and AI alignment theory; introduces novel conceptual frameworks that challenge prevailing assumptions and suggest new directions for research in neural network cognition and architecture.

# Building Better Activation Oracles

## Archive
path: rss/2026/06/lesswrong-high-karma-cb7b1a5adb.html

## Summary
### Contributions
- Improved Activation Oracle (AO) training by using on-policy rollouts and a higher-quality conversational dataset

- Introduced a small change to the activation injection formula, increasing AO accuracy and reducing hallucinations
- Developed AObench, a comprehensive evaluation benchmark for AO quality
- Demonstrated significant reduction in AO vagueness and hallucination rates
- Provided practical advice and open-sourced datasets, models, and evaluation tools for AO research

### Method
Enhanced AO training by replacing the original LatentQA dataset with a new conversational QA dataset based on unarticulated completions, feeding multiple contiguous layers of activations (layer 21-25), training on on-policy data from the target model's own generations, and adjusting the activation injection strength after the second transformer layer. Evaluations used the newly developed AObench benchmark with multiple tasks to measure hallucination, vagueness, and interpretability.

### Result
Achieved marginal improvements in AO capability, significant reductions in hallucination and vagueness, and better performance across diverse interpretability benchmarks. Provided a more user-friendly and reliable AO tool with open-source models and evaluation suites, facilitating further research in scalable, end-to-end interpretability.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to interpretability and mechanistic understanding of neural networks, emergent capabilities in large models, and AI alignment theory. Introduces novel training and evaluation methods for Activation Oracles, contributing to scalable interpretability techniques and advancing theoretical understanding of model internal representations.

# Improving LLM Code Generation via Requirement-Aware Curriculum Reinforcement Learning

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/05/2605.00433.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Proposed RECRL, a requirement-aware curriculum reinforcement learning framework for LLM code generation
- Introduced automatic perception of model-specific requirement difficulty
- Optimized challenging programming requirements to enhance training data utilization
- Developed adaptive curriculum sampling strategy for smooth difficulty variation in training batches
- Demonstrated significant performance improvements on five state-of-the-art LLMs across five code generation benchmarks

### Method
RECRL framework integrates requirement difficulty perception, requirement difficulty optimization, and adaptive curriculum sampling to improve LLM-based code generation via curriculum reinforcement learning.

### Result
RECRL achieved an average Pass@1 improvement of 1.23%-5.62% over five state-of-the-art baselines across multiple benchmarks, demonstrating significant effectiveness.

### Relevance
The work enhances LLM reasoning and training strategies relevant to AI agents and multi-agent systems by improving code generation capabilities; it provides practical curriculum learning methods applicable to agentic systems, though direct implementation details on tool use or AI memory are limited.

# ExecCritic: Learn to Test, Test to Improve for Coding Agents

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/09/2609.09133.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduced ExecCritic framework separating test generation and code repair roles for coding agents
- Developed a Test agent that learns to generate behaviorally valid tests distinguishing correct from incorrect patches
- Developed a Repair agent that revises source code using execution feedback without altering tests
- Demonstrated role-specific reinforcement learning improves agent performance on SWE-bench Verified
- Showed that independently trained Test and Repair agents achieve a 72.6% success rate, surpassing no-test baselines
- Released code publicly for reproducibility and further research

### Method
ExecCritic uses a test--verify--revise scaffold with separate Test and Repair agents based on Qwen-3.5-35B-A3B, trained via role-specific reinforcement learning to generate valid tests and improve code repair iteratively.

### Result
Post-training raised the Qwen Test agent's success from 22.2% to 62.2%; combining post-trained Test and Repair agents achieved 72.6% success on SWE-bench Verified, an 11.4-point improvement over no-test baseline without stronger models or oracle feedback.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to AI coding assistants, agentic coding workflows, AI-assisted test generation and debugging, and benchmark evaluation (SWE-bench), offering practical advances in autonomous software engineering agents and AI-driven code improvement.

# SWE-Stream: Scaling Executable Training Data for SWE Agents via Progressive Construction and Elastic Streaming

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/10/2610.20193.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Developed SWE-Stream system for scalable executable software engineering training data
- Introduced progressive construction and elastic streaming execution for task validation and refinement
- Constructed 80,874 validated tasks and collected 118,688 successful trajectories from 10,728 repositories
- Fine-tuned Qwen3-30B model achieving high resolve rates on multiple SWE-bench benchmarks
- Demonstrated superior task throughput and acceptance compared to batch and fixed-limit streaming methods
- Showcased improved AI coding agent training efficiency and effectiveness

### Method
SWE-Stream progressively validates and refines executable task candidates by reusing existing artifacts and applying targeted completion only when necessary, coordinated by an elastic scheduler that adapts execution budgets asynchronously under shared resource constraints, enabling scalable construction and streaming execution of training data from large-scale development histories.

### Result
Constructed 80,874 validated executable tasks and collected 118,688 successful trajectories from 10,728 repositories across six languages; fine-tuned Qwen3-30B model achieved resolve rates of 69.0%, 49.3%, and 45.42% on SWE-bench Verified, Multilingual, and Pro benchmarks respectively; outperformed existing data sources with 45.6% resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified; improved efficiency with 1.45× accepted-task throughput over batch construction and 13.2% more accepted tasks than fixed-limit streaming.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to AI coding assistants, autonomous software engineering agents, AI-assisted code review, test generation, debugging with LLMs, prompt engineering for code generation, SWE-bench benchmark analysis, and improving developer experience with AI tools.

# SWE-Nexus: Automated Composition of Software Engineering Tasks from Test Execution

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/10/2610.20038.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduces SWE-Nexus, an automated pipeline to construct software engineering tasks from test execution
- Develops four agents to select tests, adapt tracing, evaluate protocols, and generate behavioral specifications
- Defines a method to trace execution footprints of production functions and validate scopes via test masking
- Composes compatible scopes deterministically to form composite tasks with revalidation
- Provides a benchmark of 600 tasks from 105 repositories across six programming languages
- Evaluates 12 models under three agent scaffolds, achieving 37.8% task resolution in one attempt

### Method
SWE-Nexus uses automated agents to select test files, trace execution footprints of production functions, validate behavioral scopes by masking traced functions and observing test failures, and compose compatible scopes deterministically into composite tasks, followed by revalidation under combined masks.

### Result
A benchmark dataset of 600 atomic and composite tasks was created from 105 repositories; evaluation of 12 models showed the best configuration resolved 37.8% of tasks on first attempt, with scope-weighted scoring measuring partial recovery.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to AI coding assistants, agentic coding workflows, AI-assisted test generation, debugging with LLMs, prompt engineering for code generation, AI pair programming, IDE integrations, and autonomous software engineering agents, as it advances automated task construction from validated behaviors beyond historical changes.

# Evaluating the Impact of Explainable AI on Trust in AI-Assisted Code Review

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/07/2607.24601.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Demonstrated that Explainable AI (XAI) influences developer trust in AI-assisted code reviews
- Conducted a user study comparing three levels of XAI support in LLM-based code review systems
- Found that full explanations increase perceived trust but moderate explanations yield higher agreement with AI recommendations
- Identified that no explanations lead to lowest trust and agreement
- Showed that explanation level does not significantly affect review time
- Highlighted code readability and correctness as key reasons influencing developer decisions

### Method
Within-subjects user study with 34 participants reviewing real-world code changes using three LLM-based code review systems with varying XAI levels (detailed explanation, review feedback only, no explanations). Measured trust perceptions, agreement, reasoning, and time taken.

### Result
Full explanations yielded highest trust (3.99/5) but not highest agreement; moderate explanations achieved highest agreement (89.22%); no explanations resulted in lowest trust and agreement; explanation level did not affect review time; developers cited code readability and correctness as main decision factors.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to AI-assisted code review, AI coding assistants, and developer experience with AI tools, aligning with interests in explainability, trust, and human factors in AI-assisted software engineering.

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduced MCR-Bench, the first defect state-aware benchmark for realistic multi-round code review
- Collected 2,269 real-world multi-round code review tasks across five programming languages
- Annotated tasks with fine-grained defect metadata and dynamic state labels capturing defect evolution
- Conducted extensive experiments evaluating mainstream LLMs on defect detection and lifecycle tracking
- Identified LLM limitations in multi-round interactive code review and performance variance by defect type and severity

### Method
Developed MCR-Bench dataset with detailed annotations of multi-round code review interactions and defect states; evaluated mainstream large language models on this benchmark to assess their capabilities in defect detection and tracking across multiple review rounds.

### Result
Mainstream LLMs showed limited overall performance in multi-round defect detection and lifecycle tracking, with accuracy degrading as interaction rounds increased; performance varied significantly by defect type and severity, with complex or low-salience defects often missed; error analysis revealed critical weaknesses such as cross-round temporal misalignment and insufficient long-range memory.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to AI-assisted code review, AI coding assistants' capabilities, and evaluation of LLMs in realistic multi-round coding workflows; provides valuable insights into LLM limitations and benchmarks for improving AI pair programming, code review, and developer experience with AI tools.

## Summary
### Contributions
- Microsoft released VibeVoice, a Whisper-style speech-to-text model with built-in speaker diarization.
- VibeVoice is MIT licensed and supports transcription of audio files up to one hour in length.
- The model can be run efficiently on consumer hardware, e.g., a 128GB M5 Max MacBook Pro, transcribing one hour of audio in under 9 minutes.
- VibeVoice outputs JSON with timestamped transcriptions and speaker IDs, enabling speaker diarization and easy browsing with tools like Datasette Lite.
- The model supports multiple audio formats including .wav and .mp3 and requires token limit adjustments for longer audio.
- Splitting audio with overlap is recommended for transcribing audio longer than one hour to maintain transcription accuracy.

### Method
VibeVoice uses a Whisper-style deep learning model architecture with integrated speaker diarization, running inference via the mlx-audio toolchain and MLX-converted models on local hardware.

### Result
Efficient, accurate speech-to-text transcription with speaker diarization for up to one hour of audio, producing detailed JSON output with timestamps and speaker labels, facilitating AI-assisted audio analysis and coding workflows.

### Relevance
High relevance due to its application in AI-assisted workflows, enabling transcription and diarization that can support AI coding assistants, prompt engineering, and autonomous software engineering agents by converting spoken content into structured text data.

# Tev: Scaling Long-Horizon Agentic Environments with Dense Progress Rewards

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/10/2610.18868.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduction of Tev-Gym, a large-scale long-horizon agent training dataset with 1,170 verified task environments and dense progressive rewards
- Development of a latent-world-first approach to construct complete task specifications enabling controllable complexity and natural progress metrics
- Proposal of progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS) to convert progress into dense per-step rewards improving training efficiency
- Training of Tev-27B model achieving strong performance on long-horizon tasks, matching or surpassing leading models on ALE-CM and generalizing to Terminal-Bench benchmarks

### Method
Construct latent world specifications for tasks to generate agent-facing environments with dense progressive rewards; apply progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS) to convert progress metrics into dense per-step rewards; train large language model (Tev-27B) using this recipe on the Tev-Gym dataset.

### Result
Tev-27B achieves substantial gains on long-horizon agentic tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 on ALE-CM benchmarks, generalizing to Terminal-Bench 3.0 and 4.0 subsets surpassing GLM 5.2 and Gemini 3.7 Flash, and reaching Claude Opus 4.8-level performance on middle-horizon tasks.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to LLM-based autonomous agents, agentic frameworks, task decomposition and verification, agent evaluation and benchmarks, agentic retrieval-augmented generation, prompt engineering for agent control, and agent safety and alignment in agentic contexts.

# Are We Testing the Wrong Quantum Bugs? A Study of Fault Representation Gaps in Quantum Software Testing

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/10/2610.22089.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Audits four quantum mutation-testing tools, three curated bug benchmarks, and 410 verified bugs from ten repositories.
- Classifies faults across all sources into a shared taxonomy of 56 bug families.
- Shows that compiler transformations, type handling, and input validation are major gaps in current fault models.
- Recommends testing semantic preservation across compiler transformations and correctness at representation and component boundaries.

### Method
Empirical comparison of fault-family coverage across mutation tools, curated benchmarks, and real-world quantum software bugs collected over two years.

### Result
Mutation tools cover 20 families and benchmarks add 15, but together represent only 56 of 410 real-world bugs (13.7%). The other 354 bugs (86.3%) belong to unrepresented families; the largest gaps are compiler transformations (66), type handling (53), and input validation (47).

### Relevance
Highly relevant to testing strategy and testability: demonstrates how test artifacts can miss faults in pipelines, interfaces, and representation boundaries. The findings suggest practical improvements to fault models and benchmarks for software that transforms data or programs, including compiler-backed services.
note.title: Are We Testing the Wrong Quantum Bugs? A Study of Fault Representation Gaps in Quantum Software Testing

# Stealing Reasoning Traces from Proprietary LLM APIs

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/08/2608.09867.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Identification of an architectural vulnerability in encrypted reasoning traces across sessions and models within LLM providers.
- Development of a scalable decryption jailbreak exploiting trace compatibility to extract proprietary reasoning without direct model jailbreak.
- Demonstration of four attack vectors including anti-distillation circumvention, large-scale private data extraction, hazardous information leakage, and invisible prompt injections.
- Empirical recovery of sensitive data (PII and credentials) from publicly shared encrypted reasoning blocks across major providers.
- Proposal of cryptographic and system-level mitigations to secure client-side reasoning traces.

### Method
Exploiting the interchangeability of encrypted reasoning trace blocks across different sessions, users, and models within a provider's ecosystem by injecting encrypted traces from stronger models into weaker models to decode and output the traces in plaintext.

### Result
Successfully extracted proprietary reasoning traces, sensitive private data, and hazardous hidden information from encrypted blocks across Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google models; demonstrated new attack vectors and proposed mitigations.

### Relevance
HIGH INTEREST: The work directly impacts knowledge representation, provenance tracking, memory systems for LLMs, and retrieval-augmented generation architectures by exposing vulnerabilities in reasoning trace handling and proposing security improvements relevant to knowledge graph construction, semantic search, and memory-augmented transformers.

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/07/2607.19104.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Created SciCodePile, the largest scientific code corpus (128GB) from 37,737 public repositories
- Curated an executable benchmark of 200 scientific coding tasks with sandboxed execution and automated testing
- Evaluated 15 LLMs on scientific code generation tasks including prefix-to-suffix completion, infilling, and executable code generation
- Demonstrated current LLMs struggle with scientific code, with low CodeBLEU scores and Pass@1 rates
- Showed continued pretraining and instruction tuning on SciCodePile significantly improves scientific code generation performance

### Method
Collected and processed a large-scale scientific code corpus spanning multiple computational science disciplines; curated an executable benchmark with automated test harnesses; evaluated multiple LLMs on diverse code generation tasks; performed continued pretraining and instruction tuning experiments.

### Result
Scientific code generation remains challenging for current LLMs, with best CodeBLEU around 38 and Pass@1 at 12.3%; continued pretraining improved CodeBLEU by 2.84x and instruction tuning improved Pass@1 by 4.79x, indicating room for advancement.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to AI coding assistants and their capabilities, especially in scientific code generation, evaluation of LLMs on coding tasks, and improving AI-assisted code generation through specialized corpora and benchmarks.

# Aspire: Can Models Self-Evolve from Vague Goals?

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/08/2608.31111.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduced ASPIRE, a benchmark for vague-goal-driven self-evolution in LLM-based agents
- Designed an interactive environment supporting both model-weight and agent-harness evolution
- Provided a hidden expert-authored evaluation set of 520 items across six vague goals
- Demonstrated that vague goals shift agent focus toward goal interpretation and self-directed learning
- Showed current agents complete training loops but achieve sparse and unstable weight-level gains
- Identified challenges such as training on mismatched data and overtrusting narrow self-evaluations leading to poor transfer

### Method
Developed ASPIRE benchmark where agents receive only natural-language vague goals and must autonomously operationalize them by selecting data, update methods, training and validation signals, and evaluation timing within a unified interactive environment supporting model-weight and harness evolution.

### Result
Experiments revealed that while agents can complete iterative training and harness editing, improvements at the model-weight level are limited and unstable; agents often misinterpret goals, train on inappropriate data, and rely on narrow self-evaluations, causing local gains to fail on hidden evaluations and earlier improvements to be lost.

### Relevance
HIGH INTEREST: The work directly addresses LLM-based autonomous agents, agent self-improvement, agent evaluation benchmarks, and agentic frameworks by introducing a novel benchmark for vague-goal-driven self-evolution, aligning strongly with interests in agent autonomy, reflection, and evaluation.

# FDE-Gym: The Last Mile of AI Delivery

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/10/2610.22350.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduces FDE-Gym, a benchmark of 95 end-to-end delivery tasks across 20 customer scenarios and 18 sectors.
- Evaluates agents in simulated customer environments where they clarify requirements with stakeholders and modify production-like systems.
- Scores delivery by normalized improvement to customer success metrics, with penalties for messages, trial runs, and waiting time.
- Provides an online platform for humans to practice FDE skills under the same grading criteria.

### Method
Evaluates 13 model configurations from seven providers on expert-adapted delivery tasks, comparing realistic settings requiring discovery of unstated constraints with cases where key information is obtained.

### Result
The best configuration scores 0.56 on average and successfully resolves 14 of 95 tasks (score ≥0.8 without incident). Even when it obtains every key fact on 23 tasks, it achieves business uplift ≥0.8 on only 10, indicating that constraint discovery is a major but not sole bottleneck.

### Relevance
Strong fit: introduces an agent benchmark for realistic, interactive task delivery involving stakeholder communication, tool use, and business-outcome evaluation. It directly probes agent capability gaps beyond well-specified benchmark tasks.

# SPADE: Self-Play in Adaptive Synthetic Executable Environments

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/08/2608.19197.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduced SPADE, a self-play RL framework where a single LLM acts as both Environment Designer and Reasoning Agent
- Developed a method for the Environment Designer to generate adaptive, executable training environments with a Gym-style interface
- Proposed a regret-based optimization signal to target environments at the edge of the agent's capabilities
- Demonstrated improved performance over fixed-environment baselines across diverse benchmarks including math, science, code, and reasoning tasks
- Showed scaling benefits with larger models and improvements in multi-turn tool-use and game settings
- Highlighted the importance of grounding environment design on large pretraining corpora and accumulated environment memory

### Method
SPADE uses a single large language model in two roles: an Environment Designer that generates executable, adaptive training environments as code with reset()/step() interfaces, and a Reasoning Agent that learns to act within these environments. The Environment Designer optimizes environment difficulty by minimizing the Reasoning Agent's regret, estimated via reward gaps with and without privileged hints, enabling targeted curriculum learning.

### Result
SPADE outperforms the strongest fixed-environment baselines by an average of +5.3 across eight held-out benchmarks in math, science, code, and reasoning. It achieves +5.7 and +13.9 improvements on multi-turn tool-use benchmarks BFCL-v4 and ACEBench-Agent respectively, with performance gains increasing with model scale in game settings.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to LLM-based autonomous agents, agentic frameworks, agent memory architectures, LLM planning and chain-of-thought reasoning, tool use, agent self-improvement, agent evaluation and benchmarks, and prompt engineering for agent control. It advances agent self-improvement and environment design as a learnable component, aligning with interests in autonomous AI systems and agentic reinforcement learning.

path: arxiv/2026/07/2607.27191.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduced 'shadow evaluations' where AI agents attempt open-ended research tasks graded by original authors
- Conducted case studies on two unpublished NeurIPS 2026 papers using frontier AI agents
- Identified five key failure modes in AI agents performing open-ended research
- Demonstrated AI agents can autonomously complete engineering tasks but struggle with critical research lifecycle aspects
- Released comprehensive datasets including expert reviews, agent logs, and survey responses

### Method
Applied shadow evaluations by assigning AI agents to address central research questions of unpublished papers, with original authors grading the outputs after six days and significant compute investment.

### Result
AI agents successfully completed engineering tasks autonomously but failed to make substantial progress on open-ended research questions, leading to unambiguous rejection by authors; failure modes were consistent across models and scaffolds.

### Relevance
High relevance to LLM-based autonomous agents, agentic frameworks, agent evaluation and benchmarks, agent self-improvement and reflection, and prompt engineering for agent control; provides early evidence on capabilities and limitations of AI agents in open-ended research contexts.

# Learning Meta-Skills for Agent Harness Design in Test-Time AI4AI

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/09/2609.38143.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduced Meta-Skill concept for reusable principles in agent environment construction
- Developed a Builder model that learns to create execution harnesses for a fixed Target model
- Demonstrated improved agent performance using learned meta-skills across benchmarks
- Showed that meta-skills enable better support than direct resource delivery to the Target
- Highlighted potential for system-level self-improvement via environment learning

### Method
The Builder learns meta-skills from execution feedback on a development set, encoding when and what support to provide, then applies this frozen skill bank to construct harnesses for unseen tasks without changing model weights.

### Result
Using full-bank meta-skills improved macro-average performance by 8.95 percentage points over no-skill construction and 12.02 points over direct resource delivery, demonstrating effective translation of experience into executable support and potential for self-improving agent systems.

### Relevance
High relevance to LLM-based autonomous agents, agent harness design, reasoning-time planning, agent self-improvement, and agent evaluation; aligns strongly with interests in agentic frameworks, context management, and agent safety.

# Open-Endedness Bench: Measuring Epistemic Process from Agent Records

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/10/2610.02588.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduces OEB, a methodology to evaluate an agent's epistemic process from execution logs without relying on outcome scores or reference answers
- Compiles agent execution records into epistemic event graphs linking propositions to tested actions
- Defines four competence axes (evidence, experiment, revision, no reward hacking) and six persona traits to profile agent research habits
- Evaluates 119 runs across 12 tasks from diverse benchmarks, revealing low validity of claimed improvements and patterns in idea exploration
- Demonstrates that agent models explain more variance in persona traits than task differences

### Method
OEB reads only the agent's execution record, verifies propositions against executed actions, and constructs an epistemic event graph to score competence and persona traits without using reference answers or outcome scores.

### Result
Only 16-29% of claimed improvements by agents are supported by evidence; better runs explore more new ideas; persona traits correlate more with agent model than task.

### Relevance
HIGH INTEREST: The work evaluates how agents form, test, and revise hypotheses based on their own experience, profiling research habits and epistemic processes that reflect self-generated goals and intrinsic motivation. It measures how agents' past actions influence future behavior and goal reasoning, aligning well with interests in self-generated goals, intrinsic motivation, and continuity of intention.

- Demonstrated superior performance across 20 spatial reasoning benchmarks with 59.9% average accuracy

### Method
SpatialClaw framework uses a stateful Python kernel pre-loaded with input frames and perception/geometry primitives, allowing a vision-language model to write executable code cells stepwise, adapting analysis based on intermediate results and task demands.

### Result
Achieved 59.9% average accuracy on 20 diverse 3D/4D spatial reasoning benchmarks, outperforming recent spatial agents by 11.2 percentage points consistently across multiple VLM backbones.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to embodied AI, vision-language-action models, robot perception, and physical world understanding, advancing agentic spatial reasoning critical for humanoid robotics, robot learning, and navigation tasks.

# 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/10/2610.22341.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduces 3DCodeVerse-2M, a curated dataset of executable 3D programs packaged with source files, assets, descriptions, and verification records.
- Develops a multi-agent DAG harness that generates and refines 3D content using execution checks, spatial measurements, and visual feedback.
- Provides empirical baselines and component-level analyses, with practical guidance for 3D coding agents.

### Method
Collects and converts open-source 3D code, generates additional programs with coding agents, and uses a multi-agent harness for iterative generation and automated verification without human feedback during generation.

### Result
Fine-tuning on 3DCodeVerse-2M improves open-source models' 3D coding capabilities. The harness achieves a 90% pairwise human-evaluation win rate over Claude Design (3D Object) when both are used by Claude Opus 5.5.

### Relevance
High: directly advances multi-agent frameworks, agent harnesses, tool-based verification, and evaluation. Fine-tuning is also relevant at a medium level as it improves agent behavior on 3D coding tasks.

# CliffCompaction: Cost-Efficient Compaction for Long-Horizon Coding Agents

## Archive
path: arxiv/2026/09/2609.26779.pdf

## Summary
### Contributions
- Introduces CliffCompaction, an autocompaction technique for long-horizon coding agents
- Achieves up to 50% cost reduction under bounded context without performance loss
- Maintains fidelity by truncating/dropping content without rephrasing, preventing context drift
- Enables continual learning over sessions exceeding a million tokens with significant speedups
- Demonstrates state-of-the-art efficiency on KernelBench and improved performance-cost trade-offs on Terminal-Bench
- Provides an open-source, scaffold-agnostic API-proxy compatible with multiple agent harnesses

### Method
CliffCompaction compacts agent context by selectively truncating or dropping original content only, never rephrasing or compacting previously compacted data, thus preserving information fidelity and preventing context drift during long-horizon coding tasks.

### Result
CliffCompaction achieves up to 50% cost savings, 2.23x to 3.58x CUDA kernel speedups after 200-400 steps, surpasses specialized algorithms and trained agents on KernelBench, and improves test-time scaling efficiency, enabling agents like Kimi K2.6 to match or exceed competitors at lower cost.

### Relevance
Highly relevant to LLM-based autonomous agents, agent memory architectures, reasoning-time planning, agent harnesses and context management, agent self-improvement, and agent evaluation benchmarks. It addresses long-horizon context compaction critical for reliable, cost-efficient agent operation and continual learning, aligning closely with high-interest topics in agentic AI systems.
